Reference-signal/control overhead (CRS, PDCCH, sync) plus BLER-driven HARQ retransmissions reduce the delivered TBS/s.Q: Why is TDD DL lower than FDD at the same bandwidth? TDD time-shares one carrier between DL and UL, so only a fraction of subframes carry DL transport blocks.Further ReadingShareTechNote — Throughput Calc (FDD/TDD) — TBS-based FDD and TDD throughput examples EPC01 EPC — MME (Mobility Management Entity, control plane) EPC click to expand + What it doesThe control-plane brain of the LTE core (EPC/SAE). Terminates NAS (EMM mobility + ESM session mgmt), runs authentication (with the HSS), controls bearer setup/modify/release, triggers paging for idle UEs, handles TAU and idle-mode mobility, and orchestrates S1/handovers. It touches signalling only — never user data.InterfacesI/FToProtocol / useS1-MMEeNBS1AP — the messages you see in RCT bring-upS6aHSSDiameter — auth vectors + subscriber dataS11S-GWGTP-C — bearer/session controlS10MMEGTP-C — MME relocation (pooling)MME pool & logsMultiple MMEs form a pool area (S1-Flex) for load balancing + redundancy; an eNB connects to several. In S1AP logs the MME drives InitialContextSetup, UEContextRelease, Paging, Handover Required/Command, and returns the EMM cause on reject (see PD05).Interview Q&AQ: Does the MME carry user data? No — control plane only (NAS/S1AP/GTP-C); user data goes eNB→S-GW→P-GW.Q: What is MME pooling for? S1-Flex: several MMEs share a pool area so load is balanced and one MME failing doesn't drop the area.Further ReadingShareTechNote — SAE/EPC — MME functions and interfaces EPC02 EPC — S-GW + P-GW (user plane) EPC click to expand + The two user-plane gatewaysUser data rides GTP-U tunnels through two nodes. S-GW = the local mobility anchor; P-GW = the exit to the internet/PDN.RolesNodeKey rolesS-GWlocal mobility anchor across inter-eNB HO; terminates S1-U (GTP-U); buffers DL for idle UEs and asks MME to page; per-bearer accountingP-GWIP address allocation; PDN/internet gateway (SGi); policy enforcement via PCRF/Gx; charging; DL packet filtering (TFT); anchor for 3GPP/non-3GPPTunnels & interfacesUE -- (radio) -- eNB == S1-U (GTP-U) ==> S-GW == S5/S8 (GTP) ==> P-GW -- SGi -> Internet S5 = SGW-PGW same operator ; S8 = roaming (visited SGW home PGW)In small-cell / FHGW deployments the S-GW and P-GW are often combined (SPGW) in one node to cut latency and signalling.Interview Q&AQ: S-GW vs P-GW in one line? S-GW = mobility anchor + S1-U termination inside the operator; P-GW = IP allocation + policy/charging + the gateway to the internet.Q: What is S5 vs S8? Same GTP interface between S-GW and P-GW — S5 within one operator, S8 when roaming.Further ReadingShareTechNote — SAE/EPC — S-GW/P-GW roles, GTP-U, S5/S8 EPC03 EPC — HSS (Home Subscriber Server) EPC click to expand + What it storesThe central subscriber database: IMSI, the secret key Ki, the subscription profile (allowed APNs, QoS/AMBR), the current serving MME, and allowed PLMNs. It is the root of authentication and where "who is this SIM and what may it do" is answered.Interface & auth vectorsTalks to the MME over Diameter S6a (authentication-information, update-location, subscriber data). On request it generates the EPS AKA vector from Ki + RAND:Ki + RAND -> AUTN (network authenticates to UE) -> XRES (expected response) -> CK,IK -> KASME (root of all NAS/AS keys)The MME uses AUTN/XRES for mutual auth and derives NAS ciphering/integrity keys from K_ASME.HSS vs 5G5G splits the HSS: UDM (subscriber management) + UDR (data repository) + AUSF/ARPF (authentication). Same job, service-based. A #21 "sync failure" (PD05) is an SQN mismatch between USIM and HSS/UDM.Interview Q&AQ: Where does the authentication challenge come from? The HSS generates the AKA vector (RAND/AUTN/XRES/KASME) from Ki; the MME runs the challenge with the UE.Q: HSS equivalent in 5G? UDM (+ UDR + AUSF/ARPF) — the disaggregated, service-based version.Further ReadingShareTechNote — SAE/EPC — HSS, Diameter S6a, EPS-AKA vectors TM01 LTE Transmission Modes (TM1–TM9) MIMO click to expand + Why TMs existA transmission mode tells the UE how the downlink is being sent across antennas — single antenna, diversity, or spatial multiplexing — so it knows how to receive and what to feed back (CQI/PMI/RI).The modesTMSchemeRank / feedbackTM1Single antenna (port 0)rank 1TM2Transmit diversity (SFBC)rank 1 — robustness, no PMITM3Open-loop spatial mux (large-delay CDD)RI>1, no PMITM4Closed-loop spatial muxRI + PMI (Metro likely uses this)TM5MU-MIMOrank 1 per UETM6Closed-loop rank-1 precodingPMI, rank 1TM7/8Single/dual-layer beamforming (UE-RS)port 5 / 7,8TM9Up to 8-layer (CSI-RS + DMRS)LTE-A high-order MIMOWhich give spatial multiplexingTM3, TM4, TM8, TM9 carry >1 layer (throughput multiplication). TM2 is diversity (rank 1). Feedback: TM4 uses full CQI+PMI+RI; TM3 uses RI + CQI (no PMI); TM2 forces RI=1 (CQI only) — exactly the CSI03 behaviour.Interview Q&AQ: Which TM does a Metro AAU typically run for peak DL? TM4 (closed-loop spatial multiplexing) — it uses PMI/RI feedback to precode multiple layers.Q: Why does TM2 report no PMI? Transmit diversity is fixed (SFBC) at rank 1 — there is no precoder to choose, so only CQI (and RI=1) is reported.Further ReadingShareTechNote — LTE MIMO / TM — transmission modes, spatial multiplexing, feedback PAG01 Paging Procedure — reaching an idle UE Paging click to expand + Why it existsAn idle UE has no connection, so the network can't just send data. Paging is how the core reaches it — for mobile-terminated calls/data, SI change, or ETWS/CMAS — while the UE mostly sleeps (DRX) to save battery.DRX, PF and POUE sleeps; wakes only at its Paging Occasion (PO) in its Paging Frame (PF): PF: SFN mod T = (T div N) x (UE_ID mod N) UE_ID = IMSI mod 1024 T = min(UE-specific DRX, defaultPagingCycle) ; Ns selects the PO subframeAt the PO the UE checks PDCCH for the P-RNTI; if present it reads the paging message (PCCH) on PDSCH.Message content & responsepagingRecordList → ue-Identity (S-TMSI preferred, IMSI if needed), cn-Domain (PS/CS), plus systemInfoModification / etws-/cmas-Indication flags (see EB01). If the UE finds its identity, it launches RRC Connection Request → Service Request.Interview Q&AQ: How does a sleeping UE know when to listen? Its PF/PO are derived from its IMSI and the paging cycle, so it wakes only at those occasions to check PDCCH for P-RNTI.Q: S-TMSI vs IMSI in paging? S-TMSI is used normally (shorter, privacy); IMSI paging is a fallback (e.g. after a network failure / UE unreachable by S-TMSI).Further ReadingShareTechNote — Paging — DRX, PF/PO, P-RNTI, paging message TAU01 Tracking Area Update (TAU) Mobility click to expand + TA vs cellA Tracking Area is a group of cells; each cell broadcasts its TAC in SIB1, and TAI = PLMN + TAC. The MME gives the UE a TAI list — the UE can roam across all those TAs without signalling, which trades a slightly larger paging area for far less update traffic.Why TAU triggers• UE enters a TA not in its TAI list • periodic T3412 expiry • PLMN change • recovery. Flow:UE -> MME : TAU Request (with/without active flag) (auth if needed; S6a to HSS if MME changed) MME -> UE : TAU Accept (new TAI list, GUTI) UE -> MME : TAU CompleteActive flag & periodic TAUThe active flag in the TAU Request asks the network to also set up the user plane (piggybacked service request) so data flows immediately after the update. Periodic TAU (T3412) simply tells the MME the UE is still reachable; if it never arrives the MME may implicitly detach the UE.Interview Q&AQ: Why a TAI list instead of a single TA? It lets the UE move across many TAs without a TAU each time (less signalling) while keeping the paging area bounded.Q: What does the TAU active flag do? Requests user-plane setup along with the TAU, so the UE can send/receive data right after (no separate service request).Further ReadingShareTechNote — Tracking Area — TA/TAI list, TAU triggers and flow PDCAP Reading a Control-Plane Capture — identify protocol & procedure (S1AP/NGAP/X2AP/F1AP) Debug click to expand ▾ In plain EnglishOpen a control-plane pcap and the first two questions are: which interface/protocol is this, and which procedures are happening? Even without a full decoder, SCTP tells you the protocol by port & PPID, and one byte of each message tells you the procedure — enough to characterise any S1AP/NGAP/X2AP/F1AP trace. How it worksControl plane runs over SCTP (reliable, multi-stream). Identify the interface three ways:• SCTP port: S1AP 36412 · NGAP 38412 · X2AP 36422 · XnAP 38422 · F1AP 38472 · E1AP 38462 · E2AP 37464.• SCTP DATA chunk PPID (definitive): S1AP 18 · NGAP 60 · X2AP 27 · XnAP 61 · F1AP 62 · E1AP 64.• Procedure: each application PDU starts with a CHOICE — initiatingMessage / successfulOutcome / unsuccessfulOutcome — then the procedureCode. So one byte ≈ init/ok/fail and the next = the procedure. S1AP examples: 10=Paging, 12=initialUEMessage, 9=InitialContextSetup, 11/13=DL/UL NAS, 5=E-RABSetup, 23=UEContextRelease, 17=S1Setup, 0=HandoverPrep, 3=PathSwitchReq.What a healthy trace looks like: the association opens with S1Setup (init→success); steady Paging; per call initialUEMessage → InitialContextSetup(success) → NAS transport → E-RABSetup → UEContextRelease. Balanced init/success counts = procedures completing.Red flags: frequent Reset, an S1Setup unsuccessfulOutcome (association won't come up), or InitialContextSetup with no matching success. Tip: 127.0.0.1 loopback = internal components — filter to the real node IPs; use SCTP stream/PPID to separate interleaved procedures. Interview Q&AQ: You have a control-plane pcap but limited decode — how do you tell the interface and the procedures?
a: It's SCTP: the port identifies the interface (S1AP 36412 / NGAP 38412 / F1AP 38472 / X2AP 36422 / XnAP 38422 / E1AP 38462) and the SCTP DATA PPID confirms it (S1AP 18 / NGAP 60 / F1AP 62…). Each application PDU begins with initiating/successful/unsuccessful + a procedureCode, so you can tally procedures (Paging, InitialContextSetup, S1Setup, handover) even without full ASN.1 decode.

q: What in an S1AP/NGAP trace hints at instability?
a: Frequent Reset procedures, an S1Setup/NGSetup unsuccessfulOutcome (the eNB/gNB↔core association won't establish), or InitialContextSetup with unsuccessfulOutcome / no matching successfulOutcome. Healthy traces show a single Setup success at the start and balanced initiating↔successful counts thereafter.

Pass = throughput ≥ 95% at the reference level. RX combining gain — the number people forgetThe 3GPP number above is per single RX port. The product combines multiple RX branches, so the system-level sensitivity is better than the single-port figure by the combining gain:• Mid band (B1/B3): 4-RX combining → ≈ +6 dB• Low band incl. B28: 2-RX combining → ≈ +3 dBSo a single-port measurement of ~−104 to −105 dBm on B28 becomes ~−107 to −108 dBm after 2-RX combining. Always state which one you're quoting — comparing a single-port measurement against a combined requirement (or vice-versa) is the #1 cause of a "sensitivity looks short" false alarm. B28 has less combining headroom (3 dB) than mid-band (6 dB), so it's the first to look marginal. The isolation sequence (run in this order) 1 · Pin the firmware. Record the FHGW FW version the shortfall was seen on, and re-measure on a second FW build — rules out a FW/calibration regression before you touch hardware. 2 · +5 dB ADC attenuation, then re-measure. This is the key discriminator: • sensitivity degrades with +5 dB → not enough system gain / RX gain margin → investigate the RX gain path (LNA, front-end, DSA/ADC_ADJUST). • sensitivity ≈ unchanged with +5 dB → the ADC input level isn't the limiter → look at the DU / UL demod / BLER measurement path (decode, not RF). 3 · Change the test frequency. Move to a different (clean) in-band frequency. If it recovers, you had external RF interference, not an RU fault — verify the frequency is clean first. 4 · Compare to a reference/certification measurement. Line it up against a known-good result, but normalise first: account for the combining gain (2-RX vs single port) and any difference in the cable-loss application method — don't chase an absolute-value gap that's just a measurement convention. How the ADC-attenuation check looks at the CLIget-atten-dfe <ant> <cc> <atten×10> sets the digital front-end ADC attenuation; then inject the FRC and read power-monitor (UL dBFS), get-rssi (dBFS/dBm) and BLER. If adding attenuation barely moves BLER/sensitivity, the limit is downstream (DU/demod), not the ADC input. Interview Q&A Q: A B28 unit looks ~3 dB short on RX sensitivity — how do you debug it?
a: First check it isn't a measurement mismatch: the 3GPP number is per single RX port, but B28 uses 2-RX combining (~3 dB), so confirm I'm comparing like-for-like and normalise the cable-loss method. q: Why does mid-band have more sensitivity margin than B28?
a: Combining gain. Mid band (B1/B3) combines 4 RX branches (~6 dB), low band including B28 combines only 2 (~3 dB), so B28 has half the combining headroom and shows up marginal first.

q: What does adding ADC attenuation tell you in a sensitivity investigation?
a: It separates an RF-gain limit from a decode limit. If +5 dB of ADC attenuation worsens sensitivity, the RX chain didn't have enough gain margin; if sensitivity barely moves, the ADC input level isn't the bottleneck and the problem is downstream in the DU/UL demodulation/BLER path.

q: OBW vs ACLR? OBW measures where 99% of your power sits (containment); ACLR measures how much leaks into the neighbour channel. A clean OBW can still fail ACLR if the last 1% tail is high. FC20 Per-RFFE IQ Playback (PR 586) — isolate each RFFE × pol RCT Feature click to expand + Why it existsPer-RFFE IQ playback (PR 586 / GRDEV-8131) isolates each RF front-end module (RFFE) on each polarisation and measures ACLR/EVM per path, instead of only the combined output. Before this, TX conformance measured the summed signal from all PAs — so if one RFFE/pol was bad you couldn't tell which. Isolation turns off every path but one, so the analyzer sees just that PA. "IQ playback" = the DU replays a pre-generated IQ ETM waveform (deterministic, TX-only) rather than live PHY.How it works (tx_speed.py:771 → rffe.py)_run_iq_playback_measurements, gated on iq_playback=True AND rrh.tx_per_rffe_enabled() (rrh[0].RFFE AND rffe_control.tx_per_rffe).per ETM: connect_cli_manager -> telnet localhost:8888 (root/root, '>' prompt) per IQ port (pol A/B/C/D via iq_playback_ant_map): iq_playback {ETM.bin} {port} 0 0 ; wait 5s ; rrh.rffe_restore_all per RFFE 1..N: rffe_isolate(band,rffe,pol): mb-modify-rffe band-id: B1=1 B3=3 B8=8 B28=9928 B41=41 (TX not stopped) wait settle_sec (7s) rffe_verify_isolated -> mb-get-pa : only target ENABLED else tag ISOLATION_UNCONFIRMED _iq_measure_one -> measure_test_Tx_* (ACLR/EVM) row tagged RFFE{n}{pol}_ant{k} rffe_restore_all (at end and on failure)Modes, layout & the two quirks that make it reliableTwo modes: each-RFFE-on-each-pol (per-RFFE isolation) and all-RFFE-on-each-pol (0xf baseline, all PAs). Layout: B1/B3/B41 = "all" (4 RFFE × 4 pol = 16 paths); B8/B28 = "split" (RFFE1,2 → A,B; RFFE3,4 → C,D). Two ECS fixes make it dependable: rffe_restore_all before every measure (else RFFEs stay off → analyzer reads noise, ACLR ≈ 0 / EVM ≈ 90%) and auto-range before ACLR (else the isolated low-power path reads ACLR near the noise floor — see FC01). Run flag: --iq-playback=true. Code: source/products/rrh/mixins/rffe.py (RffeMixin), wired into FHGW.Interview Q&AQ: A per-RFFE isolated path reads ACLR 51 dBc but the combined output passes 55 — is the PA bad? Probably not — check the analyzer auto-ranged (sa_set_atten_for_min_clipping). An isolated single-PA path is lower power, so without auto-range ACLR sits near the noise floor; with it you get ~54.5–55.6.Q: How do you prove only the target RFFE was transmitting? rffe_verify_isolated reads mb-get-pa — if any non-target PA is still ENABLED the row is tagged ISOLATION_UNCONFIRMED, so a bad isolation can't silently pass. (vru.py) FWK4 Framework — S-Plane verification (PTP/SyncE timing) Framework click to expand + The "S" = Synchronization · features/tech_5g/splane_verification_nr.py · docs SPLANE_AUTOMATION_EXPLANATION.md + knowledge_base/splane_verification.md Plain English — what & whyIn an O-RAN 7.2x split the RU must keep its clock aligned to the network using PTP (IEEE-1588) driven by a Grand Master (GM), backed by GNSS + internal oscillator. Get it wrong → TDD breaks, interference, 3GPP timing fails. Two headline metrics: Frequency Error (Hz / ppb) and Time Alignment Error / TAE (ns). The RU cycles PTP states LOCKED → HOLDOVER → ACQUIRING → LOCKED. Measured by a spectrum analyzer (RF freq/time via EVM table) and a Keysight oscilloscope (physical 1PPS / 10 MHz edge). The three test typesHoldover — deliberately kill the reference (GNSS or PTP) so the RU free-runs on its oscillator, then measure drift. GM is forced to HOLDOVER before measuring so the whole window is genuine holdover. Variants: GNSS-loss, PTP-loss (C3 topology), two-GM redundancy (4 h scope capture).Stability — long capture under PTP LOCKED to build statistics (~10 samples/s) + recovery tests (re-lock after PTP restart / full reboot, e.g. "locked in 145.2s").Temperature monitoring — pre-test that waits for thermal equilibrium first, because oscillators drift with temp (TCXO ~±1 ppm/°C) and would contaminate results. Config & pre-test flowGMConfig caches the GM PTP settings (ptp_instance/ptp_port/gnss_port from setup.json "gm"). Cadence hierarchy Cadence-IDs["SPLANE"] → Group-IDs["TS_DL_SPLANE"] → Test-IDs; group carries PreTest[] + Tests[], dispatched via getattr(). Pre-test sequence: wipe FHGW logs → start PTP-packet tcpdump → temperature stabilize → PTP restart → start TX (aborts if all antennas < −20 dBm). PTP-restart polls fetch_lock_state() every 10 s until HOLDOVER, re-enables in a finally, then check_sync_state("LOCKED", timeout=600). Concrete limits & durationsmaxAbsTE < 1100 ns (3GPP, scope — abort on fail) · dTEh < 200 ns (holdover drift rate) · holdover KPIs freq_tolerance 50 ppb, time_offset 300 ns, max_time_error 1500 ns · non-holdover Freq_Error ±185 Hz, TAE 65 ns (±25), EVM 18.5%. Durations: temp stabilize 30 min (±2 °C), holdover/lock timeout 600 s, stability capture 1000 s, scope capture 4 h @ 200 ns/div. Typical "good": ±100 Hz, ±30 ns. NF1 Noise — Thermal floor kTB = −174 dBm/Hz (the absolute limit) Beginner click to expand▾ PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Thermal noise in one sentence: Any object above −273°C (absolute zero) has electrons randomly moving around — that random movement creates a tiny electrical noise. In your RU, every resistive component (cable, duplexer, LNA input) generates this noise. The LNA then amplifies it along with the wanted signal. This is why you cannot build a perfectly silent receiver. Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Thermal noise (kTB) sets the absolute noise floor. NF1 explains the physics. The full sensitivity formula using kTB + NF + SNR → DSA offset is in the DSA card. → For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Thermal Noise — kTB, Johnson-Nyquist, Noise Voltage Johnson-Nyquist Noise Source: random electron motion in resistor Power: P = kTB watts Voltage: Vn = √(4kTBR) volts Independent of resistance value Present in every resistive element in your RU In Your RX Chain Cable termination: generates kTB noise Duplexer resistive loss: generates noise LNA input resistance: generates noise LNA amplifies all of the above Cannot be eliminated — only minimised by design Key Values kTB at 290K, 1Hz: −174 dBm/Hz +10 MHz BW (+70dB): −104 dBm +System NF 5.75dB: −98.25 dBm +SNR_req −1dB: −99.25 dBm = B1 10MHz QPSK sensitivity RCT bench setup — DU, AAU, instruments, connections decoded Your bench setup — instrument roles: EXM E6640A: Vector Signal Generator. Why thermal noise is unavoidable Thermal noise and the sensitivity floor: Any resistive element above 0 K generates thermal noise. In your RX chain: the cable termination, the duplexer, the LNA input — all generate kTB noise. The LNA then amplifies both the incoming signal and all the noise it sees. You cannot eliminate this noise — you can only minimise the noise added after the signal enters the chain (which is what good LNA design does). This is why cryogenic receivers used in radio astronomy cool the LNA to near 0 K — it is the only way to get below the room-temperature kTB floor. Noise voltage — how it appears on a spectrum analyser: Noise voltage Vn = √(4kTBR). For a 50Ω system at 290K in 1MHz bandwidth: Vn = √(4 × 1.38e-23 × 290 × 1e6 × 50) = 0.895 μV = −107 dBm. On your EXA with preamp ON, this appears as the noise floor — the flat baseline across the span. When you inject a signal that rises above this floor, you can measure it. When the signal drops below it, it is lost in the noise. 📐 Real numbers — how temperature changes thermal noise −40°C T = 233K kTB = −175.6 dBm/Hz 1.6 dB better than 290K +17°C T = 290K (reference) kTB = −174 dBm/Hz 3GPP reference temp +55°C T = 328K kTB = −173.5 dBm/Hz 0.5 dB worse +70°C T = 343K kTB = −173.3 dBm/Hz 0.7 dB worse + PA derates The thermal noise change with temperature is small (LNA NF increases and PA gain decreases — both effects are larger than the thermal noise change itself. NF2 Noise — Figure (NF): SNR degradation, Noise Factor, sensitivity Intermediate click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: NF is the SNR degradation caused by your RX chain. It is the third term in the sensitivity formula after kTB+BW. Your system NF = 5.75 dB built up from the Friis chain — see NCH card. Full sensitivity derivation is in DSA card. → For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Noise Figure — SNR Degradation Through Your RX Chain NF Definition NF (dB) = SNR_in (dB) − SNR_out (dB) = how much SNR the device degrades Perfect device: NF = 0 dB (no degradation) Real cable 2.5dB loss: NF = 2.5 dB Your system: NF = 5.75 dB total (B1) NF in Sensitivity Formula Sens = −174 + 10·log(BW) + NF + SNR_req NF = 5.75 → Sens shifts 5.75 dB worse Perfect RX (NF=0): sens = −104+(−1) = −105 Real RX (NF=5.75): sens = −99.25 dBm 5.75 dB penalty vs theoretical perfect RX NF as SNR degradation — what it means in practice Noise Factor vs Noise Figure: Noise Factor (F) is the linear ratio: F = SNR_in / SNR_out. Always ≥ 1. A perfect device has F = 1. Noise Figure (NF) = 10·log(F) in dB. A perfect device has NF = 0 dB. Your system NF of 5.75 dB means F = 10^(5.75/10) = 3.76 — your chain degrades SNR by a factor of 3.76 (not 5.75 times — remember dB is logarithmic). The sensitivity formula uses NF in dB because all other terms are already in dB. How NF directly sets your test injection level: EXM injects at sensitivity threshold. Sensitivity = kTB_floor + NF + SNR_req. If your NF increases by 1 dB (e.g. cable gets longer, LNA degrades), sensitivity worsens by 1 dB, and EXM must inject 1 dB more power. If EXM is not recalibrated but NF increased, the test is now 1 dB too easy — you are testing above threshold without knowing it. This is why the DSA table is recalculated whenever hardware changes. NF3 Noise — Friis cascade (why the LNA dominates) Advanced click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Friis cascade formula explains how your 5.75 dB system NF is built from individual component NFs. This NF feeds directly into the sensitivity formula. See DSA card for full chain, NCH card for numerical calculation. → For the complete chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Friis Cascade — NF_total = NF1 + (NF2-1)/G1 + (NF3-1)/(G1·G2) + ... Before LNA G1 ≤ 1 (passive loss) Full NF penalty Cable+Dup+BPF = 3.3 dB LNA ★ NF=2 dB · G=+20 dB Dominates system NF Place ASAP in chain G=100 linear After LNA G1=100, divide NF 7dB mixer → 0.07dB Completely negligible Key design rules from Friis: 1. First stage NF dominates — LNA quality is critical 2. Minimise ALL loss before LNA (cable, connectors, filters) 3. High LNA gain shields everything after it from noise 4. Improving post-LNA components gives near-zero benefit Why Friis means you only need to care about the LNA The Friis insight — one worked example: Imagine you have a 7 dB NF mixer after your 20 dB gain LNA. Its Friis contribution is (F_mixer − 1) / G_LNA = (5.012 − 1) / 100 = 0.040 linear = 0.17 dB to system NF. Now replace that mixer with a perfect 0 dB NF mixer. System NF improvement = 0.17 dB. Barely measurable. But reduce cable loss before the LNA by 0.5 dB — system NF improves by exactly 0.5 dB, directly improving sensitivity by 0.5 dB. This is the Friis insight: optimise before the LNA, not after it. In your lab: the pre-LNA components you can actually change: The duplexer and pre-BPF are fixed inside the RFFE — you cannot change them. The LNA is a fixed chip — you cannot swap it. The only pre-LNA component you control in the test setup is the cable from EXM to the RU port. Shorter, lower-loss cable = better system NF in your measurement = better apparent sensitivity. This is why cable quality and measured loss matter, and why the VNA cable loss measurement is step 1 of every sensitivity test setup. NF4 Noise — Passive devices (attenuators, cables, filters add noise) Intermediate click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Passive devices add NF equal to their loss — this directly worsens system NF and therefore sensitivity. Every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA = 0.1 dB worse sensitivity. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. NF of Passive Devices — Golden Rule: NF (dB) = Loss (dB) Every passive device with X dB loss adds exactly X dB to system NF — no exceptions Attenuator 10 dB pad NF = 10 dB Use AFTER LNA only Before LNA = disaster Lab cable 2.5 dB loss NF = 2.5 dB Before LNA = full hit Biggest lab variable Duplexer 0.5 dB loss NF = 0.5 dB Always before LNA Cannot move it BPF Filter 0.3 dB loss NF = 0.3 dB Post-LNA: ÷100 = 0.003 Negligible after LNA Same 10 dB attenuator: Before LNA → +10 dB NF After LNA → +0.1 dB NF LNA gain divides all downstream NF by 100× For TX measurements: always put the 30 dB pad AFTER the coupler output (BOB SMA) — never in the RX path Why passive devices add noise equal to their loss A resistor at room temperature generates thermal noise power = kTB. When a passive component like a cable attenuates a signal by X dB, it absorbs part of the signal power and replaces it with its own thermal noise. The result: the signal level drops by X dB but the noise floor drops by less (because the component adds its own noise). The net effect is exactly X dB of SNR degradation, which is the definition of X dB noise figure. Why position relative to LNA is everything: The Friis formula shows that each stage's NF contribution is divided by the gain of all preceding stages. A component before the LNA (G_preceding = 1 or less) adds its full NF. A component after the LNA (G_preceding = 100 for +20 dB LNA) adds only 1/100th of its NF to the system total. This is why the design rule is: minimise all loss before the LNA, and place the LNA as early in the chain as physically possible. Your duplexer and pre-BPF must be before the LNA for functional reasons (they select the band) but their loss directly degrades sensitivity. Attenuator placement — the most common lab mistake: When measuring TX power with EXA, you add a 30 dB attenuator to protect the EXA from the strong TX signal. This attenuator must go between the RU TX output and the EXA input — never between the signal source and the RU RX input. If you accidentally put the 30 dB pad in the RX path during a sensitivity test, you add 30 dB to system NF, and your measured sensitivity becomes 30 dB worse than reality. Always double-check the signal path before running any RX measurement. Connector loss — the hidden NF contributor: A single SMA connector in good condition has approximately 0.1–0.15 dB insertion loss. That is 0.1–0.15 dB of NF contribution if it is before the LNA. In a chain with 4 connectors before the LNA (source → cable → two adapters → RU port), that is 0.4–0.6 dB of additional NF from connectors alone. A damaged or incorrectly torqued connector can have 0.3–0.5 dB extra loss, immediately visible as sensitivity degradation. This is why the VNA connector inspection checklist exists and why torque specs matter for RF measurements. NF5 Noise — The 5 types (thermal, shot, flicker/1f, white, burst) Advanced click to expand▾ Quick link — how this connects to DSA: 5 noise types exist. Thermal noise (kTB) is what the sensitivity formula is based on. Phase noise limits EVM. Quantisation noise limits ADC dynamic range. All three affect your daily measurements. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. 5 Types of Noise — Sources, Spectrum, Your Lab Impact ① Thermal kTB · Johnson-Nyquist Flat — always present Your main sensitivity floor cause Reduce: narrow BW ② Shot Discrete electrons Flat — in diodes/BJTs In your LNA biasing circuit — small Reduce: lower current ③ Flicker (1/f) Low-freq crystal defects High at low f, flat at RF GaN PA issue <1 MHz Upconverts to LO skirts Reduce: GaAs over Si ④ Phase Noise LO frequency jitter Skirts around carrier Causes EVM floor Limits 64QAM/256QAM Reduce: better VCO/PLL ⑤ Quantisation ADC rounding error Flat — white-like SQNR = 6N+1.76 dB 12-bit → 74 dB Reduce: more ADC bits The three noise types that matter most in your work Of the five noise types, three are directly relevant to your daily testing. Thermal noise sets your sensitivity floor and is the subject of the entire DSA/NF calculation chain. Phase noise from the LO limits EVM and prevents high-order modulations from decoding. Quantisation noise from the ADC sets the dynamic range ceiling. ① Thermal noise — your sensitivity floor: Generated by any resistive element at temperature above 0 K. Formula: P = kTB. In your RX chain, every lossy component (cable, duplexer, filter) generates thermal noise equal to its loss in power. The LNA amplifies both the signal and all the noise it sees, but its own added noise is small (NF = 2 dB). This is the noise the entire DSA framework is designed around — calculate it, characterise it per band, then test each band against its own correctly-adjusted threshold. ④ Phase noise — why it shows up in EVM failures: The local oscillator (LO) that downconverts your RF signal to baseband is not a perfect single frequency — it has random phase jitter. This jitter appears as noise skirts around the carrier in the frequency domain. When the LO mixes with your signal, this phase jitter gets transferred to the baseband IQ constellation — the symbol points rotate slightly randomly, which increases EVM. Phase noise is why you see an EVM floor that does not improve even when SNR is excellent. For QPSK this is not a problem, but for 64QAM and 256QAM the tighter constellation margins make phase noise the limiting factor. ⑤ Quantisation noise — ADC dynamic range: Every ADC rounds the analog signal to the nearest discrete level. With 12 bits, there are 4096 levels. The rounding error is the quantisation noise. SQNR = 6.02 × N + 1.76 = 6.02 × 12 + 1.76 = 74 dB. This means your ADC can cleanly handle signals up to 74 dB above the quantisation noise floor. If your signal swings too close to full scale (clipping), you get heavy distortion. If it is too weak (near the quantisation floor), you lose resolution. The VGA/AGC in your RX chain keeps the signal in the sweet spot — typically around −12 dBFS, well within the 74 dB dynamic range. NF Applied to Your Work — EXA Preamp, Per-Band Sensitivity Budget EXA N9010B Preamp Settings Setting DANL @ 2 GHz Atten 20 dB, preamp OFF: −103 dBm/Hz ← TX ACLR / power Atten 0 dB, preamp OFF: −120 dBm/Hz Atten 0 dB, preamp ON: −130 dBm/Hz ← RSSI / sensitivity Preamp = internal LNA — adds gain → lowers EXA's own NF NEVER use preamp for TX — overloads input → compression Rule: signal > −30 dBm → preamp OFF · signal < −60 dBm → preamp ON Per-Band Sensitivity Budget (10 MHz) Band NF(dB) Sensitivity DSA B1 2.44 −99.3 dBm 5 dB B3 2.40 −99.4 dBm 0 dB ← baseline B8 3.15 −98.6 dBm 8 dB B28 2.73 −99.0 dBm 8 dB B41 2.00 −99.8 dBm 5 dB (TDD) Sensitivity = −174 + 70 + NF + (−1) for QPSK 1/3 How NF directly drives everything in your daily test work NF is not an abstract concept — it is the single number that determines what power the EXM must inject for each band, what the EXA DANL must be to measure it, and whether a sensitivity failure is a hardware problem or a calibration issue. Every time you set up a sensitivity test, you are implicitly using NF. EXA DANL must be lower than RU sensitivity — always check: DANL (Displayed Average Noise Level) is the EXA's own noise floor — the minimum signal it can measure. For your sensitivity test to be valid, the EXA's DANL must be significantly lower than the signal you are trying to measure at the RU output. In your test: EXM injects at sensitivity threshold (e.g. −97.5 dBm at RU port after cable). The PRACH detector inside the RU processes this. You read the result via CLI (get_rssi) or DU RSSI — you are not measuring the raw RF signal with EXA at this point. The EXA is used for TX measurements. But if you ever try to measure a weak RX signal directly with EXA, the DANL check is critical: EXA DANL at −130 dBm/Hz across 10 MHz = −130 + 70 = −60 dBm — safely below your −98 dBm system noise floor. Why B8 has the highest NF (3.15 dB) and highest DSA: At 900 MHz (B8), the transistor physics in GaAs/GaN LNAs produce slightly higher noise compared to 2 GHz. Additionally, the duplexer for B8 at 900 MHz is physically larger and has higher insertion loss than at 2 GHz — the filter Q-factor degrades at lower frequencies meaning you need a wider physical filter to achieve the same selectivity, which adds loss. These two effects combine to give B8 the worst NF in your band set. B41 at 2545 MHz has the best NF (2.0 dB) because there is no duplexer — TDD uses a T/R switch which has lower loss than a duplexer. When measured sensitivity is worse than calculated — NF-based diagnosis: If your sensitivity test fails by X dB, and you have confirmed cable loss and EXM calibration are correct, the excess degradation must come from the RX chain NF being higher than assumed. Break it down: measure cable loss with VNA → subtract from EXM output → compare to sensitivity formula → if residual error > 1 dB, the RX chain NF is degraded. The most likely causes in order: (1) LNA compression from a too-strong signal on a different port, (2) LNA bias voltage wrong after firmware change, (3) duplexer damaged (cracked ceramic), (4) connector oxidised adding loss before LNA. NF_CAL Noise — NF calibration (Y-factor, ENR, hot/cold) Advanced click to expand▾ PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST NF calibration in one sentence: This is how you measure whether your LNA and RX chain are generating as little noise as expected. You inject two known noise levels (hot and cold) and measure how much noise the chain adds — that added noise is the Noise Figure. It tells you if the hardware is healthy, but it does not write any correction values. Quick link — how this connects to DSA: NF calibration uses the Y-factor method to measure actual system NF. This confirms whether NF matches the values used in the sensitivity formula. It does not write any correction — it only validates hardware health. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. NF Calibration — Y-Factor Method (Hot/Cold Noise Source) Noise Source HOT: ENR=15dB T_hot ≈ 9600 K DUT (your RU) NF = ? dB LNA + duplexer chain EXA measures N_hot = −60 dBm power in measurement BW Noise Source COLD: source OFF T_cold = 290 K DUT (your RU) same gain, same BW EXA measures N_cold = −66 dBm 6 dB lower (Y=4 linear) Y-Factor calculation: Y = N_hot / N_cold (linear) = 10^(6/10) = 3.98 ≈ 4.0 NF = ENR − 10·log(Y−1) = 15 − 10·log(3) = 15 − 4.77 = 10.2 dB ENR = Excess Noise Ratio of source Your RU measured NF targets (at RU input port, after duplexer+cable subtracted): B1: 2.44 dB B3: 2.40 dB B8: 3.15 dB B28: 2.73 dB B41: 2.00 dB What is NF calibration? NF cal answers one question: how much noise does your RX chain add to the signal? This is a hardware characterisation measurement — it tells you whether the LNA, duplexer, and cable are performing to spec. It does NOT write any correction value — it just confirms (or flags) the hardware quality. Key terms, each explained ENR — Excess Noise Ratio The "how much hotter than room temperature is the noise source" spec. ENR=15 dB means the source outputs noise equivalent to a resistor at 290 × 10^(15/10) ≈ 9200 K when switched ON. This is the known reference your calculation depends on. The noise source module has its ENR printed on it and also stored in its EEPROM so the EXA can read it automatically. Y-factor Y = N_hot / N_cold in linear power. If hot output is −60 dBm and cold output is −66 dBm, the difference is 6 dB → Y = 10^(6/10) = 3.98. The Y-factor is how much "more noise" comes out when you switch the source hot vs cold. A low Y means the DUT is adding so much noise of its own that the source temperature barely matters — i.e., high NF device. A high Y means the DUT is quiet and is faithfully amplifying the difference — i.e., low NF device. T_hot and T_cold T_cold = 290 K (standard room temperature, the IEEE reference). T_hot = 290 × 10^(ENR/10). When the noise source is OFF, it still generates thermal noise at 290 K — that becomes your cold reference. This is why you use the same physical source for both measurements: it removes cable and connector uncertainty from the result. NF formula: NF = ENR − 10·log(Y−1) Where this comes from: NF definition is SNR_in/SNR_out. For a two-port device with gain G and noise temperature T_e, the output noise is G·k·(T_cold + T_e)·B for cold input and G·k·(T_hot + T_e)·B for hot input. Taking the ratio cancels G and B, and solving for T_e gives you NF = 10·log(1 + T_e/T_0). Substituting T_e from the Y-factor ratio gives the formula above. In your lab — no standalone noise source needed The EXA N9010B has a built-in NF measurement mode under Meas → Noise Figure. It drives its own internal noise source through Port 1 output, sweeps frequencies, and automatically computes NF vs frequency. You connect EXA Port 1 → RU RX port (via calibrated cable), tell it your cable loss, and it plots NF(f) for you. You then read off the NF at your band centre (e.g. 1950 MHz for B1 UL). The EXA handles the Y-factor math internally. When NF is worse than spec — what to check If measured NF > spec by more than 1 dB: (1) Check cable loss — every 0.1 dB extra cable loss before the LNA adds 0.1 dB to measured NF. (2) Check connector torque — loose SMA can add 0.3–0.5 dB. (3) Check LNA bias — wrong supply voltage shifts NF. (4) Check for LNA compression — if signal level too high, LNA is not in its linear region and NF appears worse. (5) Duplexer damage — a damaged duplexer filter adds extra loss before the LNA, directly adding to NF. GAIN_CAL Gain calibration — RX chain ADC_ADJUST, TX power trim, what each register means Advanced click to expand▾ PLAIN ENGLISH FIRST Gain calibration in one sentence: This is how you teach the radio to report accurate power readings. You inject a signal of exactly known power, see what the radio reports, and find the offset between them. That offset (ADC_ADJUST) is saved so future readings are accurate. RX gain cal = RSSI cal — they are the same procedure called by two different names. Quick link — how this connects to DSA: Gain cal (= RSSI cal for RX, power trim for TX) corrects the difference between theoretical and actual chain gain. Gain Calibration — RX and TX Chain RX Gain Cal (finds ADC_ADJUST): EXM injects −95.0 dBm known exactly Cable −2.5 dB −97.5 RU RX chain dup+BPF+LNA +VGA+mixer ADC −12.5 dBFS get_rssi reads ADC_ADJUST = ? = P_at_RU_port − dBFS = −97.5 − (−12.5) = −85 dBm/dBFS offset Written to hardware.json: "ADC_ADJUST_B1": −85, "ADC_ADJUST_B3": −84.5, separate per band, per ADC ch TX Gain Cal (trims output power to rated target): BBU sets TX_GAIN reg integer 0-255 DAC→PA RFFE TX chain DPD+CFR active BOB SMA coupler output −16.7 dBm target EXA measures actual: −17.9 dBm error = −1.2 dB Adjust TX_GAIN +1.2 dB → increment register by ~4 counts re-measure → repeat PASS: |error| ≤ 1 dB write final reg value to tx_calibration.json TX rated targets at BOB SMA: B1=−16.7 · B3=−15.7 · B8=−18.0 · B28=−27.3 · B41=−23.0 dBm These are the power levels seen at the coupler output — full antenna power is ~30 dB higher after the coupler ratio RX Gain Calibration — what ADC_ADJUST really is The RX chain has many components between the antenna port and the ADC register: duplexer, BPF, LNA, VGA, mixer, another BPF, then the ADC. Each one has gain or loss. Rather than calibrating each component separately, RX gain cal treats the entire chain as a black box and finds one single number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any dBFS reading into an accurate dBm reading at the RU input port. ADC_ADJUST A calibration constant stored in hardware.json, one per band per ADC channel. Formula: ADC_ADJUST = P_known_at_RU_port − dBFS_reading. Once calibrated, converting any future reading is: P_dBm = dBFS + ADC_ADJUST. It absorbs the total chain gain between RU port and ADC register — so even though the LNA adds +20 dB, the VGA might be at +6 dB, and the mixer has conversion loss of −7 dB, you never need to know each individual value. The single offset does it all. Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel Each band has a different LNA gain and filter response, so the total chain gain is different per band. B1 at 2140 MHz has slightly different gain than B3 at 1843 MHz — even though they may share physical hardware, the frequency-dependent component behaviour means each band needs its own cal constant. Per ADC channel (B1 uses ADC channels 0/1/4/5, B3 uses 2/3/6/7) further accounts for ADC input impedance variation and any mismatch in the IQ paths. Temperature dependence — why RSSI can drift LNA gain changes with temperature — typically −0.02 to −0.05 dB/°C for GaAs pHEMT LNAs. In a hot lab (40°C vs 25°C calibration temp), the LNA gain drops ~0.3–0.7 dB, which makes RSSI read 0.3–0.7 dB low. If you see systematic RSSI error that grows as the RU warms up, this is why. Some RU designs have temperature compensation tables that auto-correct ADC_ADJUST as a function of measured board temperature — check hardware.json for a TEMP_COMP array. TX Gain Calibration — what TX_GAIN register controls The TX chain starts with the baseband IQ signal at full digital scale, passes through the DPD block, DAC, upconverter, PA driver, and finally the main PA. The total gain from baseband to RF output is roughly fixed by hardware, but there is always ±2–3 dB unit-to-unit variation from component tolerances. TX gain cal trims a digital attenuator (or the PA bias point) until the output power at the coupler port exactly hits the rated target. tx_calibration_eeprom.json This is the file that holds the final TX_GAIN register values after calibration — one per band per column (A/B/C/D). It is written during factory calibration and stored in the RU EEPROM. When the RU boots, it reads this file and loads the register values before enabling TX. If this file is missing or corrupt, the RU falls back to default gain values which can be 6 dB low or high — this is exactly what caused the ~6 dB B41 power deficit you found on unit 26050509 (fault 12: missing tx_calibration_eeprom.json). Coupler ratio — the BOB SMA is not antenna power The BOB SMA port is a directional coupler output, not the main antenna port. The coupler splits a small fraction of the TX power for monitoring — typically the coupling ratio is 30 dB, meaning the BOB SMA sees 30 dB less power than what goes to the antenna. So B1 rated power at BOB SMA = −16.7 dBm corresponds to +13.3 dBm at the antenna connector, or roughly 21 W EIRP per column after antenna gain. Always measure at the BOB SMA — connecting EXA directly to the antenna port would overload it instantly. DPD and its interaction with gain cal DPD (Digital Pre-Distortion) must converge before you measure TX power — it actively adjusts its coefficients for 30–60 seconds after power-on or after any power level change. If you measure output power while DPD is still adapting, you will see power fluctuating ±0.5 dB and possibly a wrong ACLR. Always wait for DPD to converge (check the DPD status register or simply wait 60 s) before taking a TX power or ACLR reading used for gain calibration. Gain cal vs RSSI cal — how they relate They are the same operation from opposite ends of the RX chain. RSSI cal (ADC_ADJUST) calibrates the entire RX path as one unit. NF cal measures just the noise-adding property of that path. TX gain cal calibrates the TX path. All three together ensure that when EXM injects −95 dBm, the RU reports −95 dBm via get_rssi, and when the BBU commands rated TX power, the antenna port outputs exactly rated power. Any mismatch between these three is a sign something has drifted or failed. Sensitivity — Power Levels on One Scale (B1, 10 MHz) kTB floor: −104 dBm (10 MHz) — pure physics, no device +NF 5.75 dB → system noise floor: −98.25 dBm SENSITIVITY: −99.25 dBm — your PRACH test threshold (B1, 10 MHz, QPSK 1/3) At this power: BLER just hits 5%. Below = link fails. Above = link works. kTB at 1 Hz: −174 dBm/Hz — absolute floor, no physics can beat this Sensitivity = −174 + 10·log(BW_Hz) + NF + SNR_required What sensitivity physically means Sensitivity is the minimum signal power at the RU antenna port at which the receiver can still decode data at 5% BLER (3GPP threshold). It is not fixed — it depends on bandwidth, modulation, and band. The sensitivity formula is not an approximation — it is an exact derivation from thermal physics and information theory. Sensitivity vs RSSI — the critical difference: Sensitivity is a threshold — the floor below which decoding fails. RSSI is a measurement — the actual received power at any instant. During a sensitivity test you set EXM to exactly the sensitivity threshold and verify the RU can decode. In normal operation RSSI is whatever arrives — could be −70 dBm (UE nearby) or −105 dBm (UE at cell edge). Sensitivity defines where the floor is. RSSI tells you where you currently are relative to that floor. Why bandwidth degrades sensitivity — the bucket analogy: A wider channel (wider bandwidth) collects more thermal noise — like a wider bucket catches more rain. The signal power stays fixed but noise increases, so SNR worsens and you need a stronger signal to decode. 5 MHz sensitivity is 3 dB better than 10 MHz. 20 MHz is 3 dB worse than 10 MHz. This is why the DSA table has separate rows for each BW — same band, different thresholds. BLER 5% — why this specific threshold: 3GPP defines sensitivity as the point where Block Error Rate = 5%. Below this, too many blocks fail and the system cannot sustain a call. At 5% BLER the link is just barely functional — this is the edge of coverage. The test is binary: inject at threshold power, count block errors, pass if BLER ≤ 5%. This is measured via the PRACH detection rate in your RCT — PRACH preamble either detected or not. This card explains what drives it: modulation order and coding rate. QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest) sensitivity — this is why FRC A1 is the standard sensitivity test. → For the complete derivation chain (kTB → NF → Sensitivity → DSA → PRACH), open the DSA card. Modulation Order vs Required SNR — Why QPSK = Best Sensitivity QPSK 1/3 4 points · 2 bits/sym SNR = −1 dB Best sensitivity FRC A1 — sensitivity test B1: −99.25 dBm Points far apart = robust 16QAM 1/2 16 points · 4 bits/sym SNR = +12 dB 13 dB worse than QPSK FRC A3 B1: −86.25 dBm Points closer = more SNR 64QAM 1/2 64 points · 6 bits/sym SNR = +18 dB 19 dB worse than QPSK FRC A5 B1: −80.25 dBm Points very close = fragile Coding rate — protection vs efficiency: Rate 1/3: 1 data bit → 3 bits sent (2/3 redundancy) Rate 1/2: 1 data bit → 2 bits sent (1/2 redundancy) Rate 3/4: 1 data bit → 1.3 bits sent (little redundancy) Lower rate = more protection = lower SNR needed = better sens Higher rate = more data = higher SNR needed = worse sensitivity Sensitivity test always uses QPSK 1/3 (FRC A1) — max protection High MCS (64QAM 3/4) used for peak throughput tests, not sensitivity What is FRC and why it determines sensitivity FRC (Fixed Reference Channel) is a 3GPP-defined test waveform with fixed modulation, coding rate, and resource allocation. Different FRCs test different capabilities. FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) tests sensitivity because it gives the most robust link — maximum coverage, minimum signal requirement. The sensitivity number you compare against in your DSA table is always FRC A1. Why QPSK 1/3 gives the best (lowest dBm) sensitivity: QPSK has only 4 constellation points — they are spread far apart in the IQ plane. Even with heavy noise, the receiver can correctly decide which of the 4 quadrants the received symbol falls in. The 1/3 coding rate adds heavy redundancy — for every bit of data, 2 extra error-correction bits are sent. Together these give an effective SNR requirement of −1 dB, meaning the signal can be 1 dB below the thermal noise floor and still be decoded. This is why QPSK 1/3 gives the best sensitivity and is the standard for coverage-limited testing. It solves the problem of testing multiple bands with one test framework: each band has a different sensitivity because each band's hardware (LNA, duplexer, filter) has different noise figures. Rather than hardcoding different thresholds manually, DSA calculates a per-band offset from the sensitivity formula and instructs EXM to inject exactly the right power for each band automatically. Step 1 — kTB: the physics floor kTB = Boltzmann constant × Temperature × Bandwidth. At room temperature (290 K), in a 1 Hz bandwidth: kTB = 1.38×10⁻²³ × 290 × 1 = 4×10⁻²¹ W = −174 dBm/Hz. This is the absolute minimum noise any receiver can have — it cannot be beaten. For your 10 MHz channel: add 10·log(10,000,000) = +70 dB → noise floor = −104 dBm. For 5 MHz: +67 dB → −107 dBm. For 20 MHz: +73 dB → −101 dBm. Every 2× increase in bandwidth raises the noise floor by 3 dB. Step 2 — System NF: what your hardware adds Noise Figure is how many dB of extra noise your RX chain adds on top of kTB. Your chain (B1): cable 2.5 dB + duplexer 0.5 dB + pre-BPF 0.3 dB + LNA 2.0 dB + post-LNA components ≈0 dB = 5.75 dB system NF. The Friis formula shows that LNA dominates because everything after it gets divided by LNA's linear gain (×100). Everything before the LNA (cable, duplexer, BPF) adds its full loss as NF — this is why cable length matters enormously for sensitivity. Per-band NF: B1=2.44 dB · B3=2.40 dB · B8=3.15 dB · B28=2.73 dB · B41=2.00 dB. B8 highest because 900 MHz LNA has higher noise, and the B8 duplexer has more loss at lower frequency. B41 lowest because TDD uses a T/R switch instead of a duplexer — less loss before the LNA. Step 3 — Sensitivity: combining it all Sensitivity = kTB_floor + 10·log(BW) + NF + SNR_required SNR_required depends on modulation and coding rate. For FRC A1 (QPSK 1/3) — the standard sensitivity test — SNR_req = −1 dB. QPSK has only 4 constellation points spread far apart, so the receiver can decode it even when signal is 1 dB below the noise floor. B1 worked example: −174 + 70 + 5.75 + (−1) = −99.25 dBm B3 baseline: −174 + 70 + 5.71 + (−1) = −99.29 dBm (slightly better NF) B8 worst: −174 + 70 + 6.46 + (−1) = −98.54 dBm (higher NF = worse sensitivity) Step 4 — DSA offset: per-band correction B3 is the reference baseline (DSA = 0). For every other band: DSA = Sensitivity_band − Sensitivity_B3. This gives the number of extra dB EXM must inject for that band to hit the correct threshold. The DSA values in your table (5 for B1, 8 for B8/B28) also include empirical corrections for path configuration differences (LB uses 2 RX paths vs HB 4 paths), flavour-specific gain settings, and actual measured hardware performance — not just the theoretical NF difference alone. Step 5 — RX paths: what rev5/rev1/comb mean Your AAU is 4T4R — 4 independent RX columns (A, B, C, D), each with its own LNA, cable, and ADC channel. rev5 = Column A tested alone (single path, worst case for that column) rev1 = Column B tested alone (independent verification of second chain) comb rev3 = Columns A+B+C combined via MRC (Maximum Ratio Combining). MRC weights each chain by its SNR and sums them. Gain ≈ +3 to 4 dB over single path. comb rev1 = All 4 columns A+B+C+D via MRC. Best possible. Gain ≈ +5 to 6 dB. Why test single paths? Because MRC hides individual column failures. If Column C's LNA is dead, comb rev1 might still pass — A, B, D compensate. The rev5/rev1 single-path tests catch dead columns that combined results would mask. This is exactly what happened with AAU #510 — B1C and B1D showed dead in single-path but combined was degraded not zero. Step 6 — before vs after: the 0.2–0.5 dB gap explained In the DSA table, every measurement has a "before" and "after" value. The DSA offset is already applied before this comparison — these are NOT showing the DSA offset itself. before = theoretical sensitivity from the formula (what physics says it should be) after = sensitivity measured on real hardware after DSA correction The 0.2–0.5 dB gap = hardware residual: connector insertion loss variation (±0.1 dB), LNA NF not exactly at datasheet (±0.1 dB), filter passband ripple (±0.05 dB), cable slightly different from assumed (±0.1 dB). A healthy unit shows consistent 0.2–0.5 dB residual across all paths. A gap suddenly becoming 2–3 dB on one path = hardware fault on that specific column. This is how you catch degraded LNAs and bad connectors at the measurement level without disconnecting anything. 📐 DSA Worked Calculation — B8 vs B3 reference (step by step) Step 1: Compute sensitivity per band Base: kTB = −174 dBm/Hz BW(10MHz) = +70 dB → floor = −104 dBm B3: NF=2.40 → sens = −104 + 2.40 − 1 = −102.6 dBm B8: NF=3.15 → sens = −104 + 3.15 − 1 = −101.85 dBm B1: NF=5.75 → sens = −104 + 5.75 − 1 = −99.25 dBm B28: NF=3.70 → sens = −104 + 3.70 − 1 = −101.3 dBm B41: NF=2.75 → sens = −104 + 2.75 − 1 = −102.25 dBm Step 2: Compute DSA offset (vs B3 reference) DSA = Sens_band − Sens_B3 (reference) DSA_B3 = −102.6 − (−102.6) = 0 dB (reference) DSA_B8 = −101.85 − (−102.6) = +0.75 dB DSA_B1 = −99.25 − (−102.6) = +3.35 dB DSA_B28 = −101.3 − (−102.6) = +1.3 dB DSA_B41 = −102.25 − (−102.6) = +0.35 dB Positive DSA = inject more power (band is less sensitive) Step 3: How EXM uses DSA Base injection = −95 dBm (arbitrary reference). EXM actual = Base + DSA offset. B3: EXM = −95 + 0 = −95 dBm · B1: EXM = −95 + 3.35 = −91.65 dBm · B8: EXM = −95 + 0.75 = −94.25 dBm After cable loss (−2.5 dB): power at RU port = EXM − 2.5 dB B1 at RU port: −91.65 − 2.5 = −94.15 dBm → compare to sensitivity −99.25 dBm → 5.1 dB above → PRACH detects reliably What the DSA physically is (GRDEV-8102)DSA = the RFDC ADC digital step attenuator on the AAU's RX path — it sits inside the RFSoC, right in front of each ADC, and is set in the personality file rfdc.txt as an opcode-2 entry per tile/block (per ADC channel). Before GRDEV-8102 every band ran DSA = 0 dB.Why it exists: the problem is ADC over-range at the top of the RX range, not sensitivity at the bottom. At DSA=0 the ADC clipped under strong uplink and raised fault id 20 ("RX out of order" / Alarm 20); the DSA backs the signal off ADC full-scale so it stops clipping. It's almost free because the noise floor is set by the LNA at the front (Friis — first stage dominates), not by the attenuator later in the chain — so headroom at the top costs ≤ ~1 dB at the bottom. RSSI Calibration — Manual Steps, Automated via RuAuto, Pass Criterion Manual procedure (one band, one channel): EXM inject −95 dBm known get_rssi 0 read dBFS e.g. −12.5 Compute offset P_port − dBFS −97.5−(−12.5)=−85 Write hw.json ADC_ADJUST_B1 = −85 Flash to RU verify: |CLI−EXM| ≤ 1 dB ✓ Pass criterion: |CLI − EXM| ≤ 2 dB |CLI − DU| ≤ 2 dB Automated via RuAuto (rssi_cal test case in tc_cadence.json): 1. EXM sweeps −60 → −110 dBm in 5 dB steps across all B1/B3/B8/B28/B41 centre frequencies 2. At each step: read get_rssi per ADC channel + DU RSSI from testmac, compute error = EXM − cable − reading 3. Max error per band > ±2 dB → flag RSSI_CAL_FAIL → auto-update ADC_ADJUST → reflash → re-verify Separate ADC_ADJUST per band/column: B1 uses ADC ch 0,1,4,5 · B3 uses 2,3,6,7 · LB (B8/B28) uses separate ADC channels What RSSI calibration actually is RSSI calibration and RX gain calibration are the same procedure with different names. The goal is to find the single offset number — ADC_ADJUST — that converts any raw dBFS reading from the ADC into an accurate dBm power level at the RU antenna port. Once calibrated, P_dBm = dBFS_reading + ADC_ADJUST for any signal in that band. The three numbers that must agree within 2 dB: EXM output − cable loss = what arrives at the RU port (your reference, measured physically) CLI get_rssi + ADC_ADJUST = what the RU's ADC chain reports (your calibrated reading) DU testmac RSSI = what the baseband processing chain reports after FFT (another independent path) All three must agree within ±2 dB. If EXM says −97.5 dBm, CLI should report −97.5 ± 2 dBm, and DU should also report −97.5 ± 2 dBm. If CLI is accurate but DU is off, the problem is in the FHGW/baseband path. If both CLI and DU are off from EXM, the ADC_ADJUST value is wrong. Why separate ADC_ADJUST per band and per ADC channel: B1 UL (1950 MHz) and B3 UL (1747 MHz) use different LNA gain settings, different filter responses, and different ADC input stages. Even if two ADC channels share the same physical ADC chip, the analog input path leading to each channel varies. Unit-to-unit component tolerance means the ADC_ADJUST for B1 on ADC channel 0 of unit 26050509 will differ slightly from the same channel on unit 26050508. This is precisely what RSSI cal measures and corrects — it is a per-unit, per-band, per-channel characterisation. Common RSSI cal failures and root causes: CLI reads 3 dB low → ADC_ADJUST was set with a different cable. Cable got swapped. Measure new cable loss with VNA and re-run cal. CLI accurate but DU off by 2 dB → FHGW BFP decompression issue or testmac RSSI averaging window mismatch. Check FHGW firmware version. RSSI drifts as unit warms up → LNA gain is temperature-sensitive. Re-run cal at operating temperature (after 30 min warm-up), or check if temperature compensation table (TEMP_COMP in hardware.json) is configured. All bands off by same amount → EXM output power was wrong during cal. Re-verify EXM output with EXA before running cal. ADC channel mapping — which channel reads which band/column: B1 Column A → ADC channel 0 · B1 Column B → ADC channel 1 B1 Column C → ADC channel 4 · B1 Column D → ADC channel 5 B3 Column A → ADC channel 2 · B3 Column B → ADC channel 3 B3 Column C → ADC channel 6 · B3 Column D → ADC channel 7 B8/B28 use 2 RX paths (columns A and B only) → channels 0 and 1 with band-specific ADC_ADJUST values So get_rssi 0 reads B1 Column A. get_rssi 2 reads B3 Column A. This mapping is why if Column C shows a bad RSSI reading (channel 4 for B1), you know exactly which physical LNA and cable path to inspect. must doA UE with no uplink timing sends a random-access preamble; the base station must detect it and reply with a timing advance. Two error rates define the test (RCT clause 8.4): missed detection and false alarm. This is the algorithm behind the FC10 PRACH sensitivity test.Preamble = CP + Zadoff-Chu + guard — baseband generationBase sequence build: DFT → IDFT + frequency shift + CP addition → power scaling (ramp-up) → half-bin shift → configurable frequency shift (from SIB2, in units of 15 kHz subcarriers, with a resampling factor K). Bin distance is 1.25 kHz for formats 0–3.Zadoff-Chu, roots & cyclic shiftsThe signature is a Zadoff-Chu sequence — constant amplitude, one sharp autocorrelation peak, low cross-correlation. The cell broadcasts a root; the 64 signatures (preamble index 0–63) come from choosing a root u and a cyclic shift v. Shift granularity is set by Ncs, which defines the Zero-Correlation Zone (ZCZ).The Ncs / ZCZ / K / roots tradeSettingK (preambles/root)RootsEffectZCZ = 1641small allowable delay, no inter-root noiseZCZ = 12~6/7~10larger allowable delay, higher inter-root noiseAllowable delay per UE = Ncs × FFT_size / 839. Bigger cells need more allowable delay (more cyclic-shift room) → more roots → more inter-root noise. That is the core PRACH planning trade.The FlexRAN-style detectorfront endremove CP → FFT → extract PRACH subcarriers× conjugate of the root ZC (correlation)IFFT → power-delay profiledecisionNoise_est = mean(noise vector)detected if peak / Noise_est > peak-multiplierpeak position → timing advanceThe peak multiplier is the tunable threshold separating a real preamble peak from noise.In RuAutotest_Rx_PRACH plays a PRACH IQ waveform and sweeps the input power down (binary or stepped “sensitivity” search) to find the detection threshold against PRACH_KPI — your PRACH ALGO deck made executable. (See FC10 / FC08T for the trace.)Interview Q&AQ: What do the noise estimator and peak multiplier decide, and what does the peak position give you?
a: The noise estimator computes Noise_est = mean of the noise vector from the post-IFFT correlation; the peak multiplier is the threshold — a correlation peak counts as a detected preamble only if peak/Noise_est exceeds it. The position of that peak in the power-delay profile gives the timing advance sent back to the UE.

q: ZCZ=1 vs ZCZ=12 — which gives more roots and more inter-root noise, and why would you use it?
a: ZCZ=12 gives ~10 roots (K≈6–7 preambles each) and higher inter-root noise, but it also allows a larger allowable delay (Ncs×FFT/839), which bigger cells need so a distant UE’s delayed preamble still lands in its zero-correlation zone. ZCZ=1 packs all 64 preambles on one root with no inter-root noise but only a tiny allowable delay — fine for small cells.

q: Why does a fixed drain voltage waste power at low traffic, and what is the fix?
a: With OFDM the PA must be backed off to handle high PAPR, and at low occupancy it sits deep in back-off where drain efficiency is poor — yet a fixed Vdd keeps burning full drain power. Dynamic Vdd lowers the drain voltage as RB occupancy falls (e.g. B1/B3: 40→32→25 V), moving the efficiency peak to the real operating point.

q: When traffic drops, do you lower Vdd before or after the occupancy change, and why?
a: After. If you lowered Vdd before the load actually dropped, the still-high signal could be pushed into clipping and violate ACLR/EVM. Conversely, when load rises you raise Vdd first. And after any Vdd change you re-tune the CFR working point and DAC current so the radiated power and spectrum stay in spec.
